title: Exact First-Passage Time Response Theory from Steady-State Response
abstract: The mean first-passage time (MFPT) provides a universal temporal measure of transport, reaction, search, and switching processes in physical, chemical, and biological systems. Understanding how MFPTs respond to perturbations is therefore crucial for prediction and control, yet a systematic theory has been lacking. We establish a compact theoretical framework for linear and nonlinear MFPT response in continuous-time Markov processes. The key tool is an exact correspondence that maps the intrinsically transient response of MFPTs onto the steady-state response of an auxiliary system. This correspondence yields exact and universal response relations for MFPTs between arbitrary state pairs, expressed entirely in terms of unperturbed MFPTs and steady-state probabilities. We then obtain a factorized physical decomposition of the MFPT response into linear upstream, linear downstream, and nonlinear contributions. Further corollaries include response-curve inference rules, fundamental bounds on MFPT responses, analytical expressions for higher-order responses of MFPTs and steady-state probabilities, and multi-rate response formulas. Additionally, our result offers computational advantages in calculating both MFPTs and steady-state distributions. Finally, a biologically motivated folding network is analyzed, and a recently reported paradox on MFPT is clarified.
summary: This work develops an exact theory detailing how Mean First-Passage Times change when a system's transition rates are perturbed. By mapping the transient response onto steady-state calculations, the authors provide universal formulas for predicting these changes. This framework is crucial for analyzing and controlling dynamic processes in complex physical, chemical, or biological networks.
main_problem: The paper aims to establish a systematic, exact theoretical framework for understanding how the Mean First-Passage Time (MFPT) responds to external perturbations in continuous-time Markov processes.
main_result: It derives universal response relations for MFPTs—including linear and nonlinear terms—expressed entirely using unperturbed MFPTs and steady-state probabilities, providing computational advantages for prediction and control.
method: The core method involves establishing an exact correspondence that maps the transient MFPT response onto the steady-state response of a carefully constructed auxiliary system.
model_or_system: The analysis is based on continuous-time Markov processes governed by the master equation, applied to systems like folding networks and general kinetic state transitions.
key_observables: Mean First-Passage Time (MFPT, $	au_{kl}$), steady-state probabilities ($\pi_k$), and their derivatives/responses to rate perturbations.
important_parameters: Perturbation strength ($\Delta W_{mn}$), unperturbed MFPTs, and steady-state probabilities.
main_assumptions: The theory is developed for single-rate perturbations ($W_{mn} 	o W_{mn} + \Delta W_{mn}$) in the Markov process rates.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the geometry of trap-bottleneck dynamics (Application I) and show numerical verification of finite response saturation due to screening factors ($\Sigma$).
paper_structure: The paper builds from establishing the fundamental correspondence between transient MFPT response and steady-state response, deriving exact linear/nonlinear update formulas, decomposing the nonlinear response into upstream accessibility, downstream gain/loss, and screening terms, and finally applying these tools to physical models like folding networks.
why_interesting: While focused on classical Markov processes, the rigorous mathematical framework for analyzing time-dependent non-equilibrium dynamics (like MFPTs) is highly relevant to open quantum systems where relaxation times and transition rates are key observables.

FIG. 1. Numerical verification of the exact finite single-rate update (Theorem 1). In each of the 105 iterations, an 8-state fully connected Markov chain is randomly generated with transition rates drawn uniformly from [0.01, 10]. One pair (k, l) is chosen for the MFPT, another pair (m, n) for the perturbation, and the perturbation strength is drawn uniformly from [0.01, 10]. The numerical MFPT ratio agrees with the exact prediction.
